deep.reconstruction:
Context: Chapter 10 of Euler's unfinished 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina' (Opera Postuma I, 1862) on quadratic residues modulo an odd prime divisor p. 'r is a residue' means x^2 ≡ r (mod p) is solvable. The previous page has already settled ±1 (via Fermat's little theorem and Euler's criterion), ±2 and ±3.

§342 (statements by induction).
- +4 = 2^2 is always a residue.
- (-4/p) = (-1/p).
- (5/p) = 1 iff p ≡ 1, 9, 11, 19 (mod 20), i.e. p ≡ ±1 (mod 5).
- (-5/p) = 1 iff p ≡ 1, 3, 7, 9 (mod 20).

§343 (summary table). For each a, Euler lists the reduced classes A mod 4|a| such that every prime p ≡ A (mod 4|a|) has (a/p) = 1:
- ±1 (mod 4), ±2 (mod 8), ±3 (mod 12), ±5 (mod 20), ±6 (mod 24), ±7 (mod 28), ±10 (mod 40), ±11 (mod 44), ±12 (mod 48), ±14 (mod 56), ±15 (mod 60).
- In every row exactly half of the φ(4|a|) reduced classes appear. That is: a 'Legendre symbol' (a/p) depending only on p mod 4|a|, with the residue classes forming an index-2 subgroup.
- The order of the entries reveals how Euler built the rows (my observation). For +11 he first lists the odd squares mod 44 (1, 9, 25, 5, 37), then their negatives (7, 39, 19, 35, 43). For -11 he lists the squares, then 3 times the squares (3, 15, 23, 27, 31). The -12 and -14 rows likewise list a square-type subgroup followed by a coset.

Marginal notes.
- (*): x^2 - 2y^2 has no odd prime divisors (not dividing y) other than those ≡ ±1 (mod 8).
- (**1): if x^2 = mn + r, then x^2 leaves residue r on division by both m and n. So whenever r is a residue for m, the cofactors n = (x^2 - r)/m also have r as a residue. This is a seed of reciprocity-type transfer arguments.
- (**2) table of 'provable' cases:
  - p = 4n-1: -1 is a non-residue.
  - p = 8n-1: -2 is a non-residue and +2 a residue.
  - p = 8n-3: ±2 are non-residues.
  - p = 12n-1: -3 is a non-residue and +3 a residue.
  - p = 12n-7 (≡ 5 mod 12): ±3 are non-residues.
  - p = 8n±3: +2 is a non-residue.
  - Implicit logic (mine): the non-residue facts come from Euler's theory of divisors of x^2 + ay^2, combined with -1 being a non-residue for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). For example, for p = 8n-1, (-1/p) = (-2/p) = -1, so (2/p) = +1. He notes that the case p = 8n+1 (2 a residue) cannot be obtained this way.

§344. Euler admits all this rests on induction and begins a route to proof: ±n is a residue for every prime p of the form 4nq + 1, or more generally 4nq + i^2 with i odd.
- Modern justification (mine): by quadratic reciprocity, p ↦ (±n/p) is a character mod 4n, so it takes the value 1 on squares i^2.
- The next page continues: +n is a residue for p = 4nq - i^2, and the classes form half of the reduced residues mod 4n.
errors: No numerical errors found. All 22 rows of the §343 table agree with the Legendre symbol computed via quadratic reciprocity, as do the statements of §342 and the marginal table (**2).
All statements are explicitly unproved ('tantum inductione nituntur'). §344's claim is true for primes p, but Euler gives no proof here; it is equivalent to quadratic reciprocity.

Margin (**1) is phrased loosely. The identity x^2 = mn + r trivially makes r a residue mod both m and n. The 'Ergo' transfers residuacity only to the specific cofactors n = (x^2 - r)/m, not to arbitrary n.
Implicit condition omitted throughout: p must not divide n (and p odd).

results.what: Classification of primes p by residue class mod 4|a| for which a is a quadratic residue, for a = ±1, ±2, ±3, ±5, ±6, ±7, ±10, ±11, ±12, ±14, ±15; classes form exactly half of the reduced residues mod 4|a|
results.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity in Euler's form ((a/p) depends only on p mod 4a and defines a character); tables of quadratic characters
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured from c. 1744; E164 published 1751; full statement E552, 1783); proved by Gauss 1796/1801

results.what: Supplementary law for 2 and -2: 2 is a residue iff p ≡ ±1 mod 8; -2 iff p ≡ 1, 3 mod 8; x^2 - 2y^2 has only prime divisors ≡ ±1 mod 8
Deriving (2/p) = 1 for p ≡ 7 mod 8 and (3/p) = 1 for p ≡ 11 mod 12 from (-1/p) = -1 together with the non-residuacity of -2, -3; noting that p ≡ 1 mod 8 escapes this method
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol combined with divisor theory of x^2 + ay^2

results.what: ±n is a residue for primes p = 4nq + i^2 (i odd)
results.modern_name: The quadratic character mod 4n is trivial on squares (a consequence of reciprocity)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known passage of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (published 1862), which historians routinely cite as Euler's empirical formulation of quadratic reciprocity. It parallels E164 and E552. The tables are correct and the structure (squares, then coset) is a nice detail, but nothing here is unknown or attributed to someone else.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import primerange, legendre_symbol; all(set(p % 20 for p in primerange(7, 5000) if legendre_symbol(5, p) == 1) == {1, 9, 11, 19} for _ in [0])
checkable.asserts: 5 is a QR exactly for primes ≡ 1, 9, 11, 19 mod 20

checkable.sympy: set(p % 20 for p in primerange(7, 5000) if legendre_symbol(-5 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 3, 7, 9}
checkable.asserts: -5 is a QR exactly for primes ≡ 1, 3, 7, 9 mod 20

checkable.sympy: set(p % 24 for p in primerange(5, 5000) if legendre_symbol(6, p) == 1) == {1, 5, 19, 23} and set(p % 24 for p in primerange(5, 5000) if legendre_symbol(-6 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 5, 7, 11}

set(p % 28 for p in primerange(3, 5000) if p != 7 and legendre_symbol(7, p) == 1) == {1, 3, 9, 19, 25, 27} and set(p % 28 for p in primerange(3, 5000) if p != 7 and legendre_symbol(-7 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 9, 11, 15, 23, 25}

set(p % 40 for p in primerange(7, 8000) if legendre_symbol(10, p) == 1) == {1, 3, 9, 13, 27, 31, 37, 39} and set(p % 40 for p in primerange(7, 8000) if legendre_symbol(-10 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 7, 9, 11, 13, 19, 23, 37}

set(p % 44 for p in primerange(3, 8000) if p != 11 and legendre_symbol(11, p) == 1) == {1, 9, 25, 5, 7, 37, 39, 19, 35, 43} and set(p % 44 for p in primerange(3, 8000) if p != 11 and legendre_symbol(-11 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 9, 25, 5, 37, 3, 15, 23, 27, 31}

set(p % 48 for p in primerange(5, 8000) if legendre_symbol(12, p) == 1) == {1, 11, 13, 23, 25, 35, 37, 47} and set(p % 48 for p in primerange(5, 8000) if legendre_symbol(-12 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 13, 25, 37, 7, 19, 31, 43}

set(p % 56 for p in primerange(3, 10000) if p != 7 and legendre_symbol(14, p) == 1) == {1, 5, 9, 13, 25, 45, 11, 31, 43, 47, 51, 55} and set(p % 56 for p in primerange(3, 10000) if p != 7 and legendre_symbol(-14 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 5, 9, 13, 25, 45, 3, 15, 19, 23, 27, 39}

set(p % 60 for p in primerange(7, 10000) if legendre_symbol(15, p) == 1) == {1, 7, 11, 17, 43, 49, 53, 59} and set(p % 60 for p in primerange(7, 10000) if legendre_symbol(-15 % p, p) == 1) == {1, 17, 49, 53, 19, 23, 31, 47}

checkable.asserts: The +11 row is exactly the odd squares mod 44 and their negatives (4nq ± i^2), explaining Euler's ordering

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(n % p, p) == 1 and legendre_symbol(-n % p, p) == 1 for n in range(1, 30) for p in primerange(3, 3000) if n % p and any((p - i*i) % (4*n) == 0 for i in range(1, 4*n, 2)))
checkable.asserts: §344: ±n is a QR for every prime p ≡ i^2 (mod 4n), i odd

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(2, p) == 1 for p in primerange(3, 5000) if p % 8 == 7) and all(legendre_symbol(3, p) == 1 and legendre_symbol(-3 % p, p) == -1 for p in primerange(5, 5000) if p % 12 == 11)
checkable.asserts: Margin table: 2 is a QR for p = 8n-1; for p = 12n-1, 3 is a QR and -3 is not
